data.title: Labour unions push for higher wages, job guarantees in FY28 Budget talks
data.description:
Labour-sector stakeholders on Friday sought higher minimum wages, wider social security coverage, stronger employment guarantees and measures to address youth unemployment at a pre-Budget consultation chaired by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, according to people aware of the matter.
 
Other proposals included lower goods and services tax (GST) on staffing services, gig worker protections and higher pensions.
 
The Indian Staffing Federation (ISF) proposed cutting GST on staffing and manpower supply services from 18 per cent to 5 per cent, while retaining full input tax credit. It said the current rate raised formal hiring costs by around 13 percentage points, making it less competitive against informal and gig arrangements. The proposed cut could generate 15-20 million additional formal jobs over the medium term, including 1.5-2 million in the near term. The gross tax differential was estimated at ₹28,000 crore, with a lower actual revenue impact after input tax credits.
 
ISF also sought a one-time ₹7,000 employer incentive for hiring skilled young people into their first formal jobs, subject to verified EPF enrolment and retention. It proposed extending the PM Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana by two years until July 2029, opening the PM Internship Scheme to companies with an annual turnover of at least ₹100 crore and linking stipend support to formal job conversion. Other demands included a national skilling-to-employment mission focused on placements rather than enrolments and allowing corporate social responsibility funds to finance hostels for migrant and women workers near industrial clusters.
 
The Trade Union Co-ordination Centre (TUCC) sought monthly minimum honorariums of ₹10,000 for ASHA workers, ₹15,000 for Anganwadi workers and ₹12,000 for helpers, along with EPF coverage. It also called for EPFO and ESIC benefits for construction workers, funded through state building and other construction workers' welfare cess funds, and appointment letters, minimum wages and social security for contractual railway goods shed workers. Eligible workers above 60 should receive gratuity and terminal benefits, it said.
 
TUCC proposed doubling the gratuity ceiling from ₹20 lakh to ₹40 lakh and raising the calculation from 15 to 21 days' wages for every completed year of service. It also sought welfare boards for fishermen, street vendors and transport workers, and subsidised EPF and ESIC contributions for eligible micro, small and medium enterprises, with the Centre and states sharing costs equally. Other demands included free family health insurance for lower-income households whose members had paid income tax for five consecutive years.
 
For gig workers, TUCC proposed an aggregator-funded social security fund, health insurance of up to ₹5 lakh and comprehensive accident cover, with registration through e-Shram.
 
The Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) demanded a national minimum wage of ₹42,000 per month, a publicly funded minimum income guarantee of the same amount for those outside regular wage employment and a universal monthly pension of ₹21,000 for the elderly. It also sought restoration of the Old Pension Scheme, repeal of the four labour codes and 200 days of rural employment under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, alongside an urban employment guarantee.
 
CITU criticised the ₹30,000-crore allocation under the MGNREGS head for 2026-27, against ₹88,000 crore in the previous year's revised estimates.
 
CITU further called for filling vacancies in government departments, semi-government establishments and public-sector undertakings, and time-bound regularisation of eligible contractual workers. Its other demands included a legal guarantee for minimum support prices, stronger public procurement, universal public distribution, healthcare spending of 3 per cent of GDP and education spending of 6 per cent. It also sought protection against job displacement due to artificial intelligence and automation, wealth and inheritance taxes, and higher taxation of extraordinary corporate profits.
 
The Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) also flagged youth unemployment and vacancies in state governments and public-sector undertakings, where many workers were employed on contract. It sought a proposal to fill these posts and a National Wage Policy providing for regular minimum wage revisions in line with inflation and the cost of living, with periodic tripartite reviews. It also proposed raising the income-tax threshold from ₹12 lakh to ₹20 lakh.
 
The Telangana Gig and Platform Workers' Union and the Indian Federation of App-Based Transport Workers sought a dedicated gig worker welfare board, backed by budgetary support and fixed platform contributions for every completed transaction. Citing unpredictable earnings, unsafe conditions, arbitrary rate changes and sudden account blocking, they called for fair payments, transparent platform reporting, safeguards against arbitrary termination and effective grievance redressal. They also flagged opaque algorithm-based management and limited collective bargaining rights, seeking health and accident insurance and pension benefits.

data.title: India develops 1st indigenous H5N1 vaccine to protect poultry from bird flu
data.description:
Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on Friday unveiled the country's first indigenously developed H5N1 (bird flu) vaccine to protect chickens from bird flu.
 
Officials from the Union Agriculture Ministry said the vaccine was developed by the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases in Bhopal.
 
They said this is the first-of-its-kind vaccine developed in India against the H5N1 virus of clade 2.3.2.1a of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI).
 
H5N1, or bird flu, is one of the most frequent diseases affecting India's poultry sector, leading to losses amounting to thousands of crores in both the domestic market and exports.
 
India's most recent major bird flu outbreak occurred in May 2026 in Navapur, Nandurbar district of Maharashtra, where the H5N1 strain of avian influenza led to the culling of nearly 400,000 poultry birds across 13 farms.
 
 
The outbreak was detected in commercial poultry farms, prompting a large-scale containment operation between May 1 and May 8, 2026.
 
Around 2.16 million eggs and 500 tonnes of poultry feed were destroyed. The strain was identified as highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1). Bird flu usually gains momentum with the onset of winter.
 
Meanwhile, addressing a programme organised at the Indian Council of Agricultural Research-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases in Anand Nagar, Bhopal, Shivraj Singh Chouhan said this indigenous vaccine was an important achievement for India in bird flu prevention and animal health protection.
 
"This vaccine is an example of India's self-reliance," he said while hailing the team of scientists that developed the vaccine indigenously.
 
"Bird flu causes large-scale deaths of chickens and huge economic losses to poultry farmers. The indigenous vaccine will strengthen bird flu control in India and provide protection to chickens," he said.
 
Chouhan said more than 500 outbreaks of H5N1 and H5N8 had been recorded in India since 2006, and until now, no specific vaccine had been available against the H5N1 virus.

data.title: Markets gain 2.6% on FPI inflows, rupee rally and cooling crude oil prices
data.description:
Markets gained more than 2.6 per cent over the past week due to strong foreign portfolio investor (FPI) inflows, an appreciating rupee, and easing crude oil and commodity prices, even as global stocks faced selling pressure despite a record initial public offering (IPO) by Anthropic.
 
The NSE Nifty 50 ended at 25,800.60 on Friday, up 1.12 per cent, bringing its weekly gain to 2.61 per cent. Similarly, the BSE Sensex rose 1.08 per cent on Friday to close at 83,919.71, gaining 2.85 per cent over the week.
 
Private banks lifted the Nifty 50 by 1.1 per cent on Friday, adding Rs 1.03 trillion to their market value in a single session. The Nifty opened at 25,368 and slipped to 25,345.20 intraday. It then climbed 455-odd points to close just 8 points below the day's high of 25,808.80. The index is now 2.2 per cent below its 52-week high. On the other hand, the Nifty Bank index gained 2.49 per cent to close at 64,635.20, after hitting a fresh 52-week high of 64,680.80 intraday.
 
 
Over the week, banks added Rs 3.22 trillion, nearly 90 per cent of the Rs 3.60 trillion added by all NSE-listed companies.
 
Global selling pressures and a hawkish Fed outlook pulled down commodity prices, boosting investor optimism in the Indian markets. As a result, domestic equities gained for the fourth consecutive week, rising 14 per cent over that period.
 
Sumit Singhania, head of research at Bajaj Broking, said banking stocks have emerged as the biggest drivers of the November market rally, outperforming the benchmark indices on favourable domestic and global factors. “FPIs invested a record Rs 1.01 trillion in Indian equities during the first fortnight of November, with financial services alone attracting over half of the total inflows. This renewed foreign investor interest has coincided with healthy second quarter (Q2) bank earnings and continued improvement in asset quality. Improved system-wide liquidity during Q2 has also provided a supportive backdrop for the banking sector,” he said.
 
Sustaining this momentum will depend on credit growth, deposit mobilisation, and margin stability, supported by continued earnings growth, Singhania added.
 
Broader markets were mixed. The Nifty Midcap 100 rose 0.66 per cent to 62,031.00, while the Nifty Smallcap 100 slipped 0.13 per cent to 19,443.60. The Nifty Media index fell 1.68 per cent, while India VIX rose 7.54 per cent to 17.33.
 
Osho Krishan, chief manager of technical & derivative research, Angel One, attributed the market rally to traction gained by buying momentum during the Thursday and Friday sessions, which was further reinforced by broad-based market participation and sharp stock movements. “A notable feature of the recent rally has been the Indian markets' resilience and continued decoupling from global peers, supported by sustained liquidity inflows from foreign institutional investors (FIIs). Meanwhile, visible sectoral rotation has kept market participants engaged, creating opportunities across multiple pockets of the market,” he said.
 
FIIs net bought shares worth Rs 32,647 crore in the secondary market this week, including Rs 10,308.42 crore on Friday. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs) net sold Rs 12,698 crore this week, including Rs 4,859.8 crore on Friday, according to provisional BSE data.
 
Among stocks, Max Healthcare Institute gained 14.14 per cent over the week, followed by Maruti Suzuki at 9.01 per cent, and Axis Bank at 8.64 per cent. Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles (TMPV) lost 7.32 per cent, while Tata Steel and Titan declined 4.65 per cent and 4.64 per cent, respectively.
 
The rupee appreciated 0.67 per cent to 92.675 against the US dollar, according to Bloomberg data.

data.title: Joint holders must disclose foreign bank accounts separately: I-T Dept
data.description:
The Income Tax Department on Friday clarified that all joint holders of a foreign bank account must disclose their holdings separately under the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers – Disclosure Scheme (FAST-DS) 2026, even if the account was funded entirely by one person.
 
In supplementary frequently asked questions (FAQs), the department said the value of the account would be divided among joint holders according to their respective ownership shares. If the shares are not specified, the value would be divided equally. A declaration filed by one account holder would not cover the others.
 
The clarifications come ahead of the December 31 deadline for the scheme, which was introduced in the Finance Act, 2026. It provides a one-time opportunity to disclose foreign bank accounts, shares, mutual funds, property and income from overseas sources that were not reported in income-tax returns. Those who make the disclosure and pay the prescribed amount will get protection from further tax, penalty and prosecution under the Black Money Act for the assets or income declared.
 
 
Under Category B, which covers foreign assets acquired from income on which tax has already been paid but which were not reported in income-tax returns, taxpayers have to pay a flat fee of ₹1 lakh, provided the aggregate value of the assets does not exceed ₹5 crore. However, assets funded partly through income that was not disclosed in tax returns are not eligible for this category and may attract the higher tax rate of 60 per cent.
 
On the scope of protection, the FAQs clarify that taxpayers will receive immunity only for the assets or income specifically included in their declaration. Assets and income already disclosed in earlier returns, including in Schedule FA (foreign assets), do not need to be declared again.
 
The department has also clarified that taxpayers can revise Form 1, the declaration form, only before the department issues Form 2. Once Form 2 is issued, they cannot submit another Form 1 to include assets inadvertently left out of the original declaration.
 
On valuation, foreign bank accounts will be valued on the basis of total deposits during the relevant period and not merely the balance at the end of the financial year. A difference of up to 20 per cent between the declared value and the value determined by the department is permissible for certain assets, including immovable property, subject to a valuation report from a recognised valuer. This relaxation does not apply to bank accounts.
 
For converting foreign currency into Indian rupees, taxpayers must use the prescribed exchange rate of ₹94.6543 per US dollar.
 
Amit Agarwal, senior partner at Nangia & Co LLP, said the clarifications provide much-needed certainty on joint ownership, valuation and procedural requirements.
 
“Once Form 2 accepts the declaration, taxpayers cannot file another Form 1 to add an overlooked asset. A complete reconciliation of overseas holdings is essential before filing,” he said.
 
He added that foreign bank accounts with aggregate balances not exceeding ₹20 lakh at any time during the relevant previous year, where the funds came from disclosed sources, continue to be protected and may not require a declaration under the scheme.

data.title: Working on zero wastewater discharge projects: Ecolab's Mukul Girotra
data.description:
Ultra-pure water maker Ecolab is working on several pilot projects that can cut industrial wastewater discharge to zero, especially from technologically complex industries such as semiconductor chip fabrication and electronics manufacturing, said the company's senior vice-president and general manager of the global high tech division, Mukul Girotra, said.
 Though several other projects, such as crystallisers and distillers, have achieved zero-water discharge, Ecolab aims to cut the cost of such projects as low as possible, Girotra said.
 Ecolab is working with several leading semiconductor companies on such projects and is looking to bring the learnings to India so an ecosystem for ultra-pure water is up and running as more chip fabrication projects come to the country, he said.
 Ultra-pure water usage, he said, is lower in projects that work on legacy-node silicon chip fabrication than in leading-edge chip fabrication units, Girotra said, adding that a decent-sized chip fabrication unit consumes roughly 8 million gallons of water per day.
 “For example, in leading-edge plants, you have close to 750 steps from start to finish before the chip is shipped out for packaging. Ultra-pure water is used at every step, after the deposition of every layer. For legacy-node projects, there are about 250 steps involved, so naturally the water usage is less,” he said.
 In addition to working on pilot projects that bring wastewater discharge to zero at the least possible cost, Ecolab is also working on steps to reuse and repurpose ultra-pure water as many times as possible, Girotra said.
 “There are 18 steps involved in manufacturing ultra-pure water, made from the same utility water. Now, the question is, do we let this water go out to discharge after one use? The old philosophy was to use ultra-pure water, treat it and then discharge it. Now, we use, treat, recover, reuse, and then treat and reuse again,” he said.
 Though using water is the best option for heat management in both semiconductor chip fabrication and data centres in tropical countries such as India, companies in this space will have to reduce consumption to a bare minimum through efficient recycling and reuse, he said.
 “We can use other products such as glycol, but using water is nearly 11-17 per cent more efficient in heat transfer and management,” Girotra said.

data.title: Bank of Maharashtra explores AMC business, overseas bond issue: MD & CEO
data.description:
State-owned Bank of Maharashtra (BoM) is exploring opportunities to expand into the wider financial services sector, including setting up an asset management company (AMC), its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer (MD & CEO), Nidhu Saxena, said on Thursday.
 
In December last year, the government completed a 6 per cent stake sale in the lender, reducing its holding to 73.60 per cent from 79.60 per cent.
 
Speaking on the sidelines of the CII-DFS Financing Summit, Saxena said, “We are looking at potential opportunities to grow in the wider financial sector, including the AMC business.”
 
Separately, the lender is exploring raising up to $175 million through overseas bonds before the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) concessional swap window for Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings (OFCBs) closes on December 31, 2026. The decision will depend on prevailing overseas market rates and movements in US Treasury yields.
 
 
“We are exploring the possibility of one more transaction of perhaps $175 million at most. However, we will take a call depending on how the pricing works out,” he said.
 
The bank had earlier raised $500 million through five-year senior unsecured fixed-rate notes carrying a coupon of 6.112 per cent, payable semi-annually.
 
On its GIFT City operations, Saxena said the bank’s International Banking Unit (IBU) had built a business book of around $2 billion in its first year, surpassing its initial target of $1 billion. The lender sees opportunities to raise international resources through GIFT City and expand banking services for non-resident Indians (NRIs), he added.
 
Saxena also stressed the need for alternative funding sources, including equity and debt markets, to finance India’s infrastructure requirements as the country works towards its goal of becoming a developed nation by 2047. While banks would continue to play a key role, traditional lending alone may not be sufficient to meet the country’s growing capital requirements, he said.

data.title: Sebi plans tighter tenure caps for exchange MDs, public interest directors
data.description:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday proposed a series of governance changes for market infrastructure institutions (MIIs) such as stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories.
 
The proposed changes include lower age and term limits for public interest directors (PIDs), a 12-year cap on the combined tenure of managing directors across MIIs, and a board seat for the Association of Mutual Funds in India's (AMFI's) chief executive at the repo clearing corporation.
 
The regulator has proposed cutting the maximum age of PIDs from 75 to 70 years and the cap on terms from three to two. A PID would serve two terms of three years each across MIIs.
 
 
The regulator said the role is quasi-regulatory and more demanding than that of an ordinary non-executive director, and that a narrow pool of individuals can circulate between MIIs.
 
Further, Sebi has proposed that a single term of a managing director (MD) would not exceed five years, with a maximum of two terms and eight years in one MII.
 
Across MIIs, an MD could serve three terms and 12 years in total. Those already serving as MDs would get a 15-year overall ceiling.
 
At present, an MD can serve 10 years in one MII and again at another, with no overall limit.
 
For executive directors (EDs), Sebi proposed eight years in a single MII and 16 years across MIIs.
 
As ED and MD together, the limits would be 12 years in one MII and 20 years across MIIs. Incumbent PIDs, MDs and EDs would continue until their ongoing terms end.
 
“Limits on MD tenure address key man risk. At the same time, staff of MIIs who aspire to senior executive positions should see a credible and orderly path to growth. A ceiling of 8 years as ED in a single MII, with a combined ceiling of 12 years as ED and MD, allows a career path to the top while keeping all executive tenures within known bounds,” noted Sebi.
 
PIDs may also be barred from simultaneous directorships in associates of MIIs, which are currently outside the restriction.
 
Sebi said this closes a structuring gap. The cap on statutory committee memberships per PID would be fixed at four, from the present five.
 
Sebi also proposed that AMFI's chief executive may be appointed, ex officio, to the board of AMC Repo Clearing Ltd (ARCL), which began operations in July 2023.
 
To manage conflicts, the AMFI chief would not sit on the risk management, members or regulatory oversight committees, would recuse themselves from decisions on risk parameters and default management, and would have no access to participant-level data. The appointment would be linked to further capital contribution by AMCs.

data.title: Cash transfers near ₹4 trn in FY27 as states expand direct welfare schemes
data.description:
Direct cash transfer schemes may have yielded political dividends for many states, but they are coming at a considerable fiscal cost.
 
Once seen as targeted welfare interventions, they have become among the fastest-growing components of state government expenditure, accounting for a rising share of revenue receipts and reshaping budget priorities.
 
From putting money in the hands of women and farmers to providing income support to youth and vulnerable households, states are committing larger sums to direct transfers, with the combined allocation for 128 identified unconditional cash transfer (UCT) schemes touching nearly ₹4 trillion in 2026-27.
 
According to the recent State of State Finances 2026-27 report by PRS Legislative Research, spending on subsidies and transfers increased from 16 per cent of states' revenue receipts in 2018-19 to 21 per cent in 2023-24, with transfers growing at an annualised rate of 24 per cent, twice the growth rate of subsidies. The share of unconditional cash transfers alone is estimated to rise from 0.6 per cent of GDP in FY23 to 1 per cent in FY27.
 
 
Women and social security pensioners account for almost 90 per cent of the proposed spending, reflecting a marked shift in welfare priorities towards putting money directly into the hands of households rather than relying solely on conventional subsidies and public provisioning.
 
West Bengal has emerged as the largest spender on unconditional transfers, with a combined allocation of ₹47,542 crore, followed by Karnataka at ₹40,392 crore and Maharashtra at ₹38,549 crore. In West Bengal, the total unconditional transfer allocation is higher than the state's capital outlay of ₹40,930 crore.
 
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Madhya Pradesh have also made substantial provisions, at ₹33,943 crore, ₹32,629 crore and ₹32,059 crore, respectively. Among other major states, ₹19,036 crore has been provisioned by Tamil Nadu, ₹18,415 crore by Odisha, ₹18,146 crore by Rajasthan and ₹16,450 crore by Kerala.
 
Women account for the largest share
 
Women have emerged as the principal beneficiaries of the new wave of unconditional transfers. West Bengal leads the country with an allocation of ₹36,000 crore for women in 2026-27, followed by Karnataka at ₹28,608 crore and Maharashtra at ₹26,500 crore. Madhya Pradesh ranks fourth with ₹23,883 crore, while Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand and Odisha have earmarked ₹14,414 crore, ₹14,066 crore and ₹10,145 crore, respectively.
 
Punjab, with an allocation of ₹9,300 crore, ranks eighth, ahead of Bihar at ₹9,052 crore, Chhattisgarh at ₹8,200 crore, Haryana at ₹6,500 crore, Delhi at ₹5,110 crore and Assam at ₹3,700 crore.
 
States have launched different schemes based on their respective allocations. While it is Lakshmir Bhandar in West Bengal and Gruha Lakshmi in Karnataka, the scheme is known as Ladki Bahin in Maharashtra and Ladli Behna in Madhya Pradesh. Odisha's Subhadra scheme, Tamil Nadu's Magalir Urimai Thogai and Jharkhand's Maiyan Samman Yojana are also part of this expanding network of women-focused assistance.
 
The schemes have gained prominence since 2023. Madhya Pradesh's Ladli Behna, Karnataka's Gruha Lakshmi and Tamil Nadu's Magalir Urimai Thogai were introduced that year, followed by major initiatives in Maharashtra, Odisha and Jharkhand in 2024. Punjab introduced a women-focused unconditional transfer scheme in 2026-27, while Kerala and West Bengal have increased allocations to their existing programmes.
 
The report pointed out that West Bengal and Jharkhand are spending an estimated 11 per cent and 10 per cent of their revenue receipts, respectively, on women-focused transfers, the highest proportions among states. West Bengal also topped the states in terms of overall direct cash transfers, accounting for around 15 per cent of revenue receipts, followed by Andhra Pradesh and Telangana at 14 per cent, Karnataka and Jharkhand at 13 per cent, and Rajasthan at 12 per cent.
 
Telangana leads farmer assistance
 
The distribution of farmer-oriented transfers presents a different picture. Telangana has made the highest allocation at ₹18,000 crore, substantially ahead of Andhra Pradesh, which ranks second with ₹6,600 crore. Maharashtra follows with ₹6,060 crore, Madhya Pradesh with ₹5,501 crore and West Bengal with ₹5,425 crore.
 
Odisha has earmarked ₹2,030 crore, while Rajasthan has provided ₹1,974 crore. Chhattisgarh's allocation stands at ₹600 crore. The allocations are for direct farm income support in states where agricultural households face uncertain earnings, rising input costs and vulnerability to weather and market fluctuations. Telangana's Rythu Bharosa, Andhra Pradesh's Annadata Sukhibhava, Maharashtra's Namo Shetkari Mahasanman Nidhi and Odisha's CM-Kisan have been supplementing the Centre's PM-Kisan assistance with their own programmes.
 
Such transfers provide farmers with a predictable source of additional income, although their effectiveness in addressing structural agricultural distress depends on whether they are accompanied by investments in irrigation, storage, market infrastructure and better price realisation, the report stated.
 
Pensions remain a major component
 
While women-focused schemes dominate the political discourse around cash transfers, social security pensions account for an equally significant part of state welfare commitments.
 
The PRS report estimates that social security pensions will account for around 0.39 per cent of GDP in 2026-27, compared with 0.5 per cent for women-focused transfers. Farmer assistance accounts for approximately 0.12 per cent and youth transfers just 0.01 per cent.
 
Fourteen states have budgeted to spend more than three-fourths of their total UCT allocation on social security pensions. In Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya, pensions account for almost the entire unconditional transfer expenditure.
 
Andhra Pradesh leads the states with ₹27,343 crore, followed by Rajasthan with ₹16,172 crore, Telangana with ₹14,629 crore, Kerala with ₹14,500 crore, Uttar Pradesh with ₹13,604 crore and Karnataka with ₹11,184 crore.
 
In contrast, women-focused schemes constitute the majority of UCT spending in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Transfers are generally disbursed monthly in most women-centric schemes, whereas programmes such as Odisha's women and farmer assistance schemes provide money in two or three instalments annually.
 
Youth receive a relatively small share
 
Direct cash assistance to young people remains a much smaller component of state welfare spending. Only five states have specific allocations, with West Bengal leading at ₹2,020 crore, followed by Karnataka at ₹600 crore, Haryana at ₹370 crore and Assam at ₹119 crore. Tamil Nadu has allocated ₹8 crore. West Bengal's allocation is significant, accounting for a large share of the total spending identified for youth across states.
 
The relatively small allocations indicate that governments have been more inclined to use direct transfers to support women and farmers than to provide unconditional assistance to youth.
 
The 16th Finance Commission has already flagged the growing fiscal burden associated with unconditional transfers, particularly where beneficiary coverage is large and targeting is weak.
 
In its assessment, the Commission observed that unconditional transfer schemes tend to have a large and untargeted beneficiary base and can impose a substantial fiscal burden. It recommended rationalising beneficiary coverage to improve the efficiency of expenditure.
 
Amarendra Das, associate professor at the National Institute of Science Education and Research (NISER), said UCTs are not confined to one political party or region. Governments across the country have adopted direct benefit transfers for women, farmers and vulnerable sections, including elderly people, widows and persons with disabilities. But the scale and composition of spending vary considerably, depending on the political priorities and social protection framework of individual states, he added.

data.title: CAG to audit city finances under World Bank-backed urban governance project
data.description:
The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) is training its officers to audit how cities raise revenue, borrow and manage their finances under a World Bank non-lending technical assistance project to strengthen its audit capacity in the urban sector.
 
World Bank acting country director for India Paul Procee said the partnership is meant to enable better quality of service delivery and support the government's initiatives to enhance public trust.
 
The project, titled 'Strengthening Audit Capacity and Governance Accountability in India's Urban Sector', is endorsed by the Department of Economic Affairs. The training was held as a two-day workshop on urban infrastructure financing and municipal finance in New Delhi and concluded on Friday.
 
 
The training workshop comes as the CAG has embarked on the audit of 101 cities, with a different theme each year. The audit has begun with urban mobility this year, to be followed by water and sanitation, housing, air quality management and liveable urban environments in the following years. “These audits will provide a holistic and comparable view of how cities are performing,” said CAG K Sanjay Murthy in a statement.
 
According to a workshop note, India's urban finance landscape is becoming more complex as urbanisation accelerates and infrastructure needs expand.
 
Cities continue to depend substantially on intergovernmental transfers and public programmes, it said. But the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions and the Urban Challenge Fund are placing greater emphasis on own-source revenue, financial discipline, project bankability and market-based finance.
 
This requires cities to strengthen their revenue base, improve accounting and financial reporting, develop financially viable projects and show they can service their borrowings.
 
"These developments have direct implications for public audit," the note said. Audit planning and checklists may increasingly need to examine borrowing and debt-servicing capacity, contingent liabilities, project bankability, revenue collection and the quality of municipal accounts.
 
Murthy called for a sectoral approach so that the multiple verticals of the urban sector are assessed holistically. He said the delivery of services to citizens must stay central to the audit.
 
One of the programme's stated objectives is to broaden the audit focus from transactions and expenditure to outputs, outcomes, value for money, asset sustainability and service delivery, "without entering the executive decision-making domain".
 The workshop sessions covered municipal revenue and finances, financial reforms and cost recovery, the delivery of urban services and innovative methods of financing, drawing on case studies from India alongside international best practices.

data.title: Sebi proposes removing additional disclosure framework for FPIs
data.description:
In a bid to attract more foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday proposed removing the Additional Disclosure Framework (ADF) for such overseas investors, which was introduced in August 2023 for granular disclosure on ultimate beneficial owners.
 
This comes against the backdrop of large FPI outflows which have exerted severe pressure on the foreign exchange market and the value of the Indian rupee.
 
Sebi noted that such disclosure requirements may act as “entry barriers” for FPIs and need to be weighed against the prevailing requirements in other jurisdictions “competing for the same pool of global monies”.
 
 
“The granular disclosure requirements under ADF have been prescribed by Sebi over and above the BO (beneficial owners) identification requirements specified under PMLR (Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005). Further, such granular disclosure requirements under the ADF are unique to India,” the regulator noted.
 
Under the current requirements, if FPIs meet specified concentration or size criteria, they are mandated to submit granular details of all entities holding any ownership, economic interest or exercising control — on a full look-through basis upto all natural persons without any thresholds.
 
These include FPIs that hold more than 50 per cent of their Indian equity assets under management (AUM) in a single corporate group, or those whose individual or combined holdings with their investor group exceed ₹50,000 crore in Indian equity markets.
 
The threshold was raised from ₹25,000 crore to ₹50,000 crore in April 2025. However, exemptions were provided to certain broad-based, pooled funds with diversified investor bases and those with government or government-related ownership, subject to specified conditions.
 
 Under PMLR, the threshold for controlling ownership is 10 per cent and 15 per cent depending on the legal form of the client — thresholds also applicable to FPIs.
 
Sebi added that several developed markets follow a 25 per cent threshold with lower thresholds only for high-risk entities.
 
“Thus, going by global standards, India follows a more stringent regime for identification of BOs. There may be a need to review the PMLR, 2005 to make it consistent with other jurisdictions. However, this is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance,” noted Sebi.
 
FPIs have been net sellers in the Indian equity markets for a sustained period starting late 2024 — accelerating in the subsequent years, Sebi noted. It added that while there could have been several factors behind FPI outflows, the “relatively onerous rules” on identification and disclosure of BOs compared to other countries necessitated a review.  
 
“Many foreign investors looking to invest in India consider the granular disclosure requirements as an additional compliance burden. Rather than investing in India and be subject to granular disclosures, many investors may instead choose to avoid investing in India,” noted Sebi.
 
The additional disclosure framework came months after the now defunct Hindenburg Research levelled allegations of violations of minimum public shareholding and stock manipulation against the Adani group — which were denied by the ports-to- retail conglomerate.
 
In its discussions with the FPIs, Sebi noted some of the challenges raised by overseas investors included collecting information from a significantly larger number of underlying investors for India specific investments, requirement to set up different fund for India investments owing to different compliance levels, frequent change in investor holdings in pooled vehicles such as hedge funds, and difficulty in tracing ownership in structures such as fund of funds.
 
“Disclosure requirements that are not in line with globally accepted practices could potentially place India at a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis peer jurisdictions with relatively lenient regulatory requirements,” noted the paper.
